title: How do you work with compound growth and CAGR without a calculator?
description: Compound growth explained for case interviews: CAGR, quick multipliers, the rule of 72, and a table of growth factors you can memorise.
hook: Treat growth as multiplication, not addition: 10% a year for two years is 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.21, or 21%, not 20%. CAGR is the single yearly rate that turns the start value into the end value, and without a calculator you find it with a few memorised growth factors, a guess-and-test step and the rule of 72.
body:
The idea

Each year's growth builds on the last year's total. A company growing 10% a year from $100M gains $10M in year one, $11M in year two and $12.1M in year three, ending at $133.1M. The total increase is 33.1%, not 30%.

CAGR, the compound annual growth rate, runs this backwards. It is the constant yearly rate that would take you from the start value to the end value:

CAGR = (end ÷ start)^(1 ÷ years) − 1

You will rarely calculate the root exactly in an interview. Instead, use one of the methods below.

Growth factors worth memorising

Yearly growthAfter 3 yearsAfter 5 yearsAfter 10 years
5%×1.16×1.28×1.63
10%×1.33×1.61×2.59
15%×1.52×2.01×4.05
20%×1.73×2.49×6.19

Three ways to find CAGR without a calculator

1. Look it up in the table

Revenue grew from $100M to $161M in five years, a factor of 1.61. The table says 10% for five years gives ×1.61, so the CAGR is 10%.

2. Bracket and interpolate

Revenue tripled from $100M to $300M over ten years. The table says 10% gives ×2.59 and 15% gives ×4.05, so the answer is between them and closer to 10%. Test 12%: 1.12¹⁰ = 3.11, just above 3. So the CAGR is a little under 12% (11.6% exactly). See the guess-and-test method for more.

3. Count doublings with the rule of 72

Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ growth rate. If a market doubled in six years, it grew about 72 ÷ 6 = 12% a year. If it quadrupled in twelve years, that is two doublings in twelve years, so again about 12%. See the rule of 72.

Averaging versus compounding

Dividing total growth by the number of years always overstates the CAGR. From $100M to $133.1M over three years, 33.1% ÷ 3 = 11.0%, but the true rate is 10%. The error grows with the rate and the period.

The opposite error happens when you forecast. If you add a fixed amount each year instead of compounding, you understate the end value. Forecasting $100M at 10% a year as "$10M a year for three years" gives $130M instead of $133.1M.

Falls and recoveries are not symmetric

A 20% fall needs a 25% rise to get back to where it started (1 ÷ 0.8 = 1.25). A 50% fall needs a 100% rise. When a client says "we lost 20% last year but grew 20% this year", they are still 4% below where they began (0.8 × 1.2 = 0.96).

Is the historical CAGR the right number to use?

A clean calculation is only as good as the history behind it. Suppose revenue grew from $200M to $260M over three years: a CAGR of 9.1%. But $30M of the end figure came from an acquisition. Organic revenue went from $200M to $230M, a CAGR of only 4.8%. Projecting 9.1% forward would roughly double the true underlying growth rate.

Strong: "Revenue grew at about 9% a year, but stripping out the acquisition, organic growth was under 5%. I'd use about 5% for the forecast, unless the client plans more deals."
Weak: "It grew $60M in three years, so $20M a year, which is 10%. I'll forecast 10% a year."

Ask too whether growth came from price or volume, and whether a single exceptional year is driving the average. In a growth case, the quality of the forecast rests on these assumptions more than on the arithmetic.

Common mistakes

  • Dividing total growth by the years to get an annual rate.
  • Adding yearly rates instead of multiplying factors.
  • Assuming a fall and an equal rise cancel out.
  • Extrapolating reported growth without removing acquisitions or one-offs.

Practice

1. Sales grew from $25M to $40M over three years. What is the CAGR?

Show the answer

The factor is 1.6. The table gives 1.52 for 15% and 1.73 for 20%, so test 17%: 1.17³ = 1.60. CAGR is about 17%.

2. An $80M business grows 6% a year. How big is it after five years?

Show the answer

1.06⁵ = 1.34 (between the 5% factor of 1.28 and the 10% factor of 1.61, nearer the 5% end). $80M × 1.34 = about $107M.

3. Sales fell 20% last year. What growth does the client need this year to get back to where it was?

Show the answer

1 ÷ 0.8 = 1.25, so 25%. On a $100M starting point, sales fell to $80M, and $80M × 1.25 = $100M.

Where to practise next

Practise reading growth off exhibits in line charts, then build speed in the case maths drill.
